1 Preliminaries

1.1 How this course is organised

The course is built around one idea: a Bayesian analysis is a posterior distribution, and in practice we obtain posterior distributions by computing, not by integrating by hand. Mathematics is kept to what you need to understand what the computer is doing and why it can go wrong.

Lecture Topic Main computational tool Practical
1 Bayesian reasoning: prior, likelihood, posterior Grid approximation 1
2 Priors, conjugate models, posterior summaries & prediction Exact formulae + simulation 2
3 Monte Carlo and Markov chain Monte Carlo Hand-written Metropolis & Gibbs samplers in R 3
4 MCMC in practice: NIMBLE and convergence diagnostics NIMBLE, posterior 4
5 Bayesian regression, model checking, comparison, hierarchical models NIMBLE, loo 5

Longer derivations (conjugate posteriors, Jeffreys priors, the full normal model, loss functions) are in the appendices. You might be asked to derive a sonjugate prior in the exam, but for the other derivations, while they are useful for understanding and for self-study, you are not expected to be able to reproduce them in the exam.

1.2 Code notes

  • These notes have been prepared using quarto - qmd shared on GitHub.

  • All code is R; Bayesian models are specified in NIMBLE (a dialect of BUGS).

  • R packages used: tidyverse, gridExtra, HDInterval, nimble, coda, posterior, loo (plus MCMCvis optionally). Install them all before the first practical: NIMBLE needs a working C++ compiler (Rtools on Windows, Xcode command line tools on macOS).

  • Course materials: https://github.com/gitMarcH/UNIMA_STA623_2026

1.5 Notation

  • \(Y, Y_1,\ldots,Y_n\): random variables (data before they are observed); \(y, y_1,\ldots,y_n\): observed values. \(\mathbf{y}=(y_1,\ldots,y_n)\).
  • \(\theta\): a generic parameter (or vector of parameters).
  • \(p(\cdot)\): a probability mass or density function; which one is meant is clear from its argument. \(p(\theta)\) is the prior, \(p(y\mid\theta)\) the sampling model / likelihood, \(p(\theta\mid y)\) the posterior.
  • \(\theta^{(1)},\ldots,\theta^{(S)}\): \(S\) simulated draws of \(\theta\).
  • \(E[\cdot]\), \(\text{Var}(\cdot)\): expectation and variance. \(\sim_{\text{iid}}\): independent and identically distributed.
  • Distributions are parameterised as in R unless stated otherwise, e.g. \(\text{Gamma}(a,b)\) has shape \(a\) and rate \(b\) (mean \(a/b\)).

A short refresher of probability theory (axioms, random variables, expectation, joint/marginal/conditional distributions) is in Appendix A. Please read it before Lecture 1 if any of it is unfamiliar.

2 Lecture 1: Bayesian reasoning

2.1 Two ways of thinking about unknown quantities

Frequentist Bayesian
Parameter \(\theta\) Fixed, unknown constant Unknown, uncertainty described by a probability distribution
Probability means Long-run relative frequency Degree of belief (consistent with the axioms of probability)
Result of an analysis Estimator \(\hat\theta\) + sampling distribution (SE, CI, p-value) Posterior distribution \(p(\theta\mid y)\)
Uncertainty statement “95% of intervals constructed this way contain \(\theta\)” “Given model and data, \(P(\theta\in[l,u]\mid y)=0.95\)”
Prior information Used informally (design, choice of model) Used formally, through the prior \(p(\theta)\)

Both are legitimate; they answer different questions. In large samples with vague priors, they often give numerically similar answers. The Bayesian approach becomes especially attractive when:

  • we want direct probability statements about parameters (“what is the probability that the new regimen reduces mortality?”);
  • data are sparse and genuine prior information exists;
  • models are complex (hierarchical, spatial, missing data, measurement error), where Bayesian computation is often easier than maximum likelihood.

2.2 The only probability rules you need

For events \(A\) and \(B\) (see Appendix A for the full refresher):

  • Conditional probability: \(P(A\mid B)=P(A\cap B)/P(B)\), for \(P(B)>0\).
  • Multiplication rule: \(P(A\cap B)=P(A\mid B)P(B)\).
  • Law of total probability: if \(B_1,\ldots,B_k\) partition the outcome space, \(P(A)=\sum_j P(A\mid B_j)P(B_j)\).

Combining the three gives Bayes’ rule:

\[ P(B_i\mid A)=\frac{P(A\mid B_i)\,P(B_i)}{\sum_j P(A\mid B_j)\,P(B_j)}. \]

2.2.1 Example: a malaria rapid diagnostic test

A malaria RDT has sensitivity \(P(T\mid D)=0.95\) and specificity \(P(\bar T\mid\bar D)=0.90\). What is the probability that a child with a positive test actually has malaria, \(P(D\mid T)\)?

\[ P(D\mid T)=\frac{P(T\mid D)P(D)}{P(T\mid D)P(D)+P(T\mid\bar D)P(\bar D)}. \]

The answer depends on the prior probability \(P(D)\), i.e. the prevalence where the child lives. Rather than computing one number, let us compute it for every prevalence:

Code 
sens <- 0.95; spec <- 0.90
ppv <- function(prev) sens * prev / (sens * prev + (1 - spec) * (1 - prev))

tibble(prevalence = seq(0.001, 0.6, length = 500)) |>
  mutate(ppv = ppv(prevalence)) |>
  ggplot(aes(prevalence, ppv)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(0.02, 0.30), linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
  labs(x = "prior probability P(D) (prevalence)",
       y = "posterior probability P(D | T+)")
Code 
ppv(c(0.02, 0.30))
[1] 0.1623932 0.8028169

In a low-transmission setting (2% prevalence) a positive result gives only a 16% probability of malaria; in a high-transmission setting (30%) it gives 80%. Same test, same data, different prior, different conclusion. This is Bayesian inference in miniature:

\[ \underbrace{P(D\mid T)}_{\text{posterior}} \;\propto\; \underbrace{P(T\mid D)}_{\text{likelihood}}\times\underbrace{P(D)}_{\text{prior}}. \]

The denominator \(P(T)\) does not depend on the hypothesis; it just makes the posterior probabilities add up to 1.

2.3 From hypotheses to parameters

Usually the “hypotheses” are the possible values of a parameter \(\theta\), and the “evidence” is a dataset \(\mathbf{y}\). Bayes’ rule for densities is

\[ p(\theta\mid\mathbf{y})=\frac{p(\mathbf{y}\mid\theta)\,p(\theta)}{p(\mathbf{y})}, \qquad p(\mathbf{y})=\int p(\mathbf{y}\mid\theta)\,p(\theta)\,d\theta, \]

and since \(p(\mathbf{y})\) is a constant once the data are observed,

\[ \boxed{\;p(\theta\mid\mathbf{y})\;\propto\;p(\mathbf{y}\mid\theta)\,p(\theta)\;} \qquad\text{posterior}\propto\text{likelihood}\times\text{prior}. \]

Everything in this course follows from this line. The ingredients are:

  • the sampling model \(p(\mathbf{y}\mid\theta)\): how data are generated if we knew \(\theta\). Viewed as a function of \(\theta\) for fixed data it is the likelihood, the same object you use in GLMs;
  • the prior \(p(\theta)\): what we know about \(\theta\) before seeing these data;
  • the posterior \(p(\theta\mid\mathbf{y})\): what we know after seeing the data;
  • the marginal likelihood or evidence \(p(\mathbf{y})\): the normalising constant. It is usually the hard part to compute, and most computational methods in this course are designed to avoid computing it.

2.4 A first computational method: grid approximation

Example. A district health team wants to estimate the prevalence \(\pi\) of malaria parasitaemia among under-fives in a village. They test \(n=30\) children and find \(k=9\) positive. A survey two years ago in a neighbouring village suggested prevalence around 20-30%.

  • Sampling model: \(Y\mid\pi\sim\text{Bin}(n=30,\pi)\).
  • Prior: \(\pi\sim\text{Beta}(2,5)\), which has mean \(2/7\approx0.29\) and is fairly wide.

We do not need any integration to find the posterior. We can evaluate \(\text{likelihood}\times\text{prior}\) on a fine grid of values for \(\pi\) and normalise numerically:

Code 
n <- 30; k <- 9
a <- 2; b <- 5

grid <- tibble(pi = seq(0, 1, length = 1001)) |>
  mutate(prior      = dbeta(pi, a, b),
         likelihood = dbinom(k, size = n, prob = pi),
         unnorm     = likelihood * prior,
         posterior  = unnorm / sum(unnorm * 0.001))   # 0.001 = grid spacing

grid |>
  mutate(likelihood = likelihood / sum(likelihood * 0.001)) |>  # scaled for plotting only
  pivot_longer(c(prior, likelihood, posterior), names_to = "curve") |>
  mutate(curve = factor(curve, levels = c("prior", "likelihood", "posterior"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(pi, value, colour = curve)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("steelblue", "salmon", "mediumorchid")) +
  labs(x = expression(pi), y = "density", colour = NULL)

The posterior is a compromise between prior and likelihood, and it is narrower than either: combining two sources of information reduces uncertainty.

TipComputational tip: work on the log scale

With many observations, \(p(\mathbf{y}\mid\theta)\) is a product of many small numbers and underflows to 0 on a computer. Always compute \(\log p(\mathbf{y}\mid\theta)+\log p(\theta)\), subtract its maximum, and only then exponentiate. Every serious Bayesian software does this internally.

A discrete prior (e.g. “the coin is one of three coins with \(\pi=0.3,0.5,0.8\)”) is simply a grid with very few points: exactly the same code works.

2.4.1 Summarising a grid posterior by sampling

Once we have the posterior on a grid, the easiest way to summarise it is to draw samples from it. This idea (replace a distribution by a large sample from it) is the foundation of everything in Lectures 3-5.

Code 
draws <- sample(grid$pi, size = 1e5, replace = TRUE, prob = grid$posterior)

c(post_mean = mean(draws),
  post_sd   = sd(draws),
  quantile(draws, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975)),
  P_above_0.4 = mean(draws > 0.4))
  post_mean     post_sd        2.5%         50%       97.5% P_above_0.4 
 0.29719852  0.07403816  0.16400000  0.29300000  0.45200000  0.08922000

Posterior mean, standard deviation, median, 95% credible interval, and the probability that prevalence exceeds 40%: all from one line each, and no calculus.

2.5 The exact answer: conjugacy

For this particular prior/likelihood pair we can also get the posterior exactly. Keeping only factors that depend on \(\pi\):

\[ p(\pi\mid k)\;\propto\;\underbrace{\pi^{k}(1-\pi)^{n-k}}_{\text{likelihood}}\;\underbrace{\pi^{a-1}(1-\pi)^{b-1}}_{\text{prior}} =\pi^{a+k-1}(1-\pi)^{b+n-k-1}, \]

which we recognise as the kernel of a \(\text{Beta}(a+k,\;b+n-k)\) density. No integral is needed: the normalising constant must be whatever makes a Beta density integrate to 1. (The full derivation including the normalising constant is in Appendix B.1.)

When prior and posterior belong to the same family, the prior is called conjugate for the sampling model. Check that the grid agrees with the exact result:

Code 
ggplot(grid, aes(pi, posterior)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 2, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_line(aes(y = dbeta(pi, a + k, b + n - k)), colour = "mediumorchid", linetype = 2) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 0.7)) +
  labs(x = expression(pi), y = "posterior density",
       subtitle = "grey: grid approximation; dashed: exact Beta(a+k, b+n-k)")

The posterior mean is a weighted average of the prior mean and the sample proportion:

\[ E[\pi\mid k]=\frac{a+k}{a+b+n}=\underbrace{\frac{a+b}{a+b+n}}_{\text{weight on prior}}\cdot\frac{a}{a+b}+\underbrace{\frac{n}{a+b+n}}_{\text{weight on data}}\cdot\frac{k}{n}. \]

So \(a+b\) behaves like a prior sample size: the Beta(2,5) prior carries the information of about 7 children, the data carry 30.

2.6 Prior versus data

What happens as data accumulate? Keep the observed proportion at 30% and increase \(n\):

Code 
post_curves <- expand_grid(n = c(10, 30, 100, 500), pi = seq(0, 1, length = 500)) |>
  mutate(k = 0.3 * n,
         Prior = dbeta(pi, a, b),
         Posterior = dbeta(pi, a + k, b + n - k),
         `Scaled likelihood` = dbeta(pi, k + 1, n - k + 1)) |>
  pivot_longer(c(Prior, Posterior, `Scaled likelihood`), names_to = "curve")

ggplot(post_curves, aes(pi, value, colour = curve)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~ paste("n =", n), nrow = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("mediumorchid", "steelblue", "salmon")) +
  labs(x = expression(pi), y = "density", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

With more data the posterior concentrates and the likelihood dominates: different reasonable priors lead to practically the same conclusions. One exception: if the prior gives zero probability to a region, so does the posterior, no matter how much data we collect (because posterior \(\propto\) likelihood \(\times\) 0). Never put zero prior probability on values that are physically possible.

2.7 Sequential updating

Today’s posterior is tomorrow’s prior. If the team tests another 20 children and finds 4 positive, then starting from the \(\text{Beta}(11,26)\) posterior gives a \(\text{Beta}(15,42)\) posterior, which is exactly the same as analysing all 50 children at once with the original \(\text{Beta}(2,5)\) prior. Bayesian inference is coherent in this sense.

2.8 Why grids are not enough

The grid method needs the posterior evaluated at every grid point. With 100 grid points per parameter:

Parameters Grid points
1 100
2 10,000
5 1010
10 1020

A logistic regression with 10 covariates is already out of reach. This curse of dimensionality motivates Monte Carlo and MCMC (Lecture 3), which spend computational effort only where the posterior has appreciable mass.

NotePractical 1

Bayes’ rule for diagnostic tests (combining two tests); grid approximation for a binomial and a Poisson model; checking grid results against conjugate formulae; effect of prior and sample size.

3 Lecture 2: Priors, conjugate models and posterior summaries

3.1 A catalogue of conjugate models

Conjugate models give posterior distributions in closed form. They are useful for quick calculations, as building blocks inside Gibbs samplers (Lecture 3), and for checking software. You should know what they are and how to use them; the derivations are in Appendix B.

Sampling model Conjugate prior Posterior Interpretation of prior parameters
\(Y\sim\text{Bin}(n,\pi)\) \(\pi\sim\text{Beta}(a,b)\) \(\text{Beta}(a+k,\;b+n-k)\) \(a\) prior successes, \(b\) prior failures
\(Y_i\sim\text{Pois}(\lambda)\) \(\lambda\sim\text{Gamma}(a,b)\) \(\text{Gamma}(a+\sum y_i,\;b+n)\) \(a\) prior total count in \(b\) prior observations
\(Y_i\sim\text{Exp}(\lambda)\) \(\lambda\sim\text{Gamma}(a,b)\) \(\text{Gamma}(a+n,\;b+\sum y_i)\) \(a\) prior events in total time \(b\)
\(Y_i\sim\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), \(\sigma^2\) known \(\mu\sim\mathcal N(\mu_0,\tau_0^2)\) \(\mathcal N(\mu_n,\tau_n^2)\), see below \(\mu_0\) prior guess, \(\tau_0^2\) its uncertainty
\(Y_i\sim\mathcal N(\mu,1/\phi)\), \(\mu\) known precision \(\phi\sim\text{Gamma}(a,b)\) \(\text{Gamma}\left(a+\tfrac n2,\;b+\tfrac12\sum(y_i-\mu)^2\right)\)
\(\mathbf Y\sim\text{Multinom}(n,\mathbf p)\) \(\mathbf p\sim\text{Dirichlet}(\boldsymbol\alpha)\) \(\text{Dirichlet}(\boldsymbol\alpha+\mathbf y)\) \(\alpha_j\) prior counts in category \(j\)

For the normal mean with known variance:

\[ \frac{1}{\tau_n^2}=\frac{1}{\tau_0^2}+\frac{n}{\sigma^2},\qquad \mu_n=\tau_n^2\left(\frac{\mu_0}{\tau_0^2}+\frac{n\bar y}{\sigma^2}\right). \]

Posterior precision = prior precision + data precision; posterior mean = precision-weighted average of prior mean and sample mean. This pattern (weights proportional to amount of information) appears in every row of the table.

3.1.1 Example: Gamma-Poisson

Recall that if \(Y\sim \mbox{Pois}(\lambda)\), then

\[ \begin{cases} P(Y=k|\lambda) &= \frac{\lambda^ke^{-\lambda}}{k!} & \;\mbox{if }k=0,1,2\ldots\mbox{ and 0 otherwise} \\ E[Y|\lambda] &=\lambda & \\ Var(Y|\lambda) &=\lambda & \end{cases} \]

Suppose \(Y_i\sim_{\mbox{iid}} \mbox{Pois}(\lambda)\), \(i=1,\ldots,n\) and we observe data \(y_1,\ldots,y_n\).

The joint pdf of the data is given by

\[ \begin{align} p(y_1,\ldots,y_n|\lambda) &=&\prod_{i=1}^n p(y_i|\lambda) \\ &=&\prod_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{y_i!}\lambda^{y_i}e^{-\lambda} \\ &=&\frac{1}{\prod_i y_i!}\lambda^{\sum_i y_i} e^{-n\lambda} \end{align} \]

The factor \(\frac{1}{\prod_i y_i!}\) is constant for each dataset. So if we compare densities for different values of \(\lambda\), this factor will cancel out. All information about \(\lambda\) is therefore contained in \(\sum_i y_i\).

\(\sum_i y_i\) is a sufficient statistic for the parameter \(\lambda\) in the Poisson sampling model.

Posterior density

If we assume a prior distribution \(p(\lambda)\), then the posterior density for \(\lambda\) given the data is given by

\[ \begin{cases} p(\lambda|y_i,\ldots,y_n) & \propto & p(\lambda) \, p(y_1,\ldots,y_n|\lambda) \\ & \propto & p(\lambda) \, \lambda^{\sum y_i}e^{-n\lambda} \end{cases} \]

If we want \(p(\lambda)\) to be conjugate for the Poisson sampling model, i.e. we want \(p(\lambda|y_1,\ldots,y_n)\) to be in the same family of distributions as \(p(\lambda)\), then the above implies that \(p(\lambda)\) needs to include terms of the form \(\lambda^{c_1}e^{-c_2\lambda}\).

The simplest class of such distributions is the family of gamma distributions (these include only such terms).

Recall \(\Lambda\sim\Gamma(a,b)\) with parameters \(a>0, b>0\) if

\[ p(\lambda|a,b)=\begin{cases} \frac{b^a}{\Gamma(a)}\lambda^{a-1}e^{-b \lambda} &\mbox{ if }\lambda>0\\ 0 &\mbox{ otherwise} \end{cases} \]

where \(\Gamma(\alpha)=\int_0^{\infty}z^{\alpha-1}e^{-z}dz\) is the gamma function.

And

\[E(\Lambda)=\frac{a}{b},\, Var(\Lambda)=\frac{a}{b^2},\,\mbox{mode}(\Lambda)=\frac{a-1}{b}\,\mbox{ if }a>1,\, 0\mbox{ otherwise}\]

Suppose \[\begin{cases} Y_1,\ldots,Y_n\sim_{\mbox{iid}}\mbox{Pois}(\lambda) \; &\mbox{(sampling model)}\\ & \\ \lambda\sim\Gamma(a,b) &\mbox{(prior distribution)} \end{cases}\]

Then

\[ \begin{align} p(\lambda|y_1,\ldots,y_n) &\propto & p(\lambda)\,p(y_1,\ldots,y_n) \\ &\propto & \left(\lambda^{a-1}e^{-b\lambda}\right) \left(\lambda^{\sum y_i} e^{-n\lambda}\right) \\ &\propto & \lambda^{a+\sum y_i-1} e^{-(b+n)\lambda} \end{align} \]

This is a \(\Gamma(a+\sum_i y_i,b+n)\) distribution.

So we see that

\[\begin{cases} \mbox{prior }\, p(\lambda) & = \Gamma(a,b) \\ \\ \mbox{likelihood }\, p(y_i,\ldots,y_n|\lambda) & = \mbox{Pois}(\lambda) \end{cases}\]

\[\Rightarrow\mbox{posterior }\, p(\lambda|y_1,\ldots,y_n) = \Gamma(a+\sum_i y_i,b+n)\] Example: Malaria episodes in a village in Malawi

What would be a real-world research / public health setting where we could encounter this?

It turns out we could use this to model the number of malaria episodes in a rainy season in a village in Malawi.

  • Episodes in one rainy season for \(n=18\) children
  • \(\sum y_i=40\), so \(\bar y=2.22\)
  • Model: \(Y_i\mid\lambda\sim\text{Pois}(\lambda)\), independently
  • Prior: \(\lambda\sim\text{Gamma}(a,b)\)

The number of malaria episodes recorded for 18 children over one rainy season:

Code 
y <- c(1, 3, 2, 3, 0, 2, 6, 4, 4, 1, 1, 3, 2, 3, 1, 1, 3, 0)
c(n = length(y), sum = sum(y), mean = mean(y))
        n       sum      mean 
18.000000 40.000000  2.222222

With \(Y_i\mid\lambda\sim_{\text{iid}}\text{Pois}(\lambda)\) and prior \(\lambda\sim\text{Gamma}(a,b)\):

\[ p(\lambda\mid\mathbf y)\propto\underbrace{\lambda^{\sum y_i}e^{-n\lambda}}_{\text{likelihood}}\;\underbrace{\lambda^{a-1}e^{-b\lambda}}_{\text{prior}} =\lambda^{a+\sum y_i-1}e^{-(b+n)\lambda}\;\Rightarrow\;\lambda\mid\mathbf y\sim\text{Gamma}\left(a+\textstyle\sum y_i,\;b+n\right). \]

Note that the data enter only through \(n\) and \(\sum y_i\) (a sufficient statistic). With a \(\text{Gamma}(5,2)\) prior (prior mean 2.5 episodes, worth about 2 children’s data), the posterior is \(\text{Gamma}(45, 20)\).

3.2 Choosing a prior

There is no single “correct” prior. There are, however, good and bad ways of choosing one, and the choice should always be stated, justified and checked.

3.2.1 Types of prior

  • Informative priors encode substantive knowledge: a previous study, a meta-analysis, a biological constraint, expert opinion. A convenient way to build one: choose a prior mean \(m\) and an equivalent prior sample size \(n_0\), then for your choice of parametric distribution, select parameters so that the prior distribution has mean \(m\) and an information content equivalent to \(n_0\). E.g. for a proportion use \(\text{Beta}(m n_0,\,(1-m)n_0)\). Opinions from several experts can be pooled as a mixture of their priors.
  • Weakly informative priors rule out implausible values without imposing a specific guess, e.g. a log-odds ratio of 10 (odds ratio \(\approx\) 22,000) is not plausible for most exposures, so \(\mathcal N(0,1.5^2)\) on a log-odds ratio is a sensible default. These are the recommended defaults for most regression parameters.
  • Vague / “non-informative” / reference priors try to let the data speak. Examples are uniform priors and Jeffreys priors \(p_J(\theta)\propto\sqrt{I(\theta)}\), where \(I(\theta)\) is the Fisher information (Appendix B.3). Jeffreys priors are invariant to reparameterisation; for the binomial the Jeffreys prior is \(\text{Beta}(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)\), for the Poisson it is \(p(\lambda)\propto\lambda^{-1/2}\), which is improper (does not integrate to 1). Improper priors can be used only if the resulting posterior is proper, which must be checked.
WarningA flat prior is not an uninformative prior

A prior that is flat on one scale is not flat on another. A uniform prior on a prevalence \(\pi\) implies a far-from-flat prior on the log-odds \(\text{logit}(\pi)\). Conversely, the very common “vague” prior \(\mathcal N(0,100^2)\) on a log-odds puts about 90% of its mass on prevalences below 0.001% or above 99.999%:

Code 
tibble(`Uniform(0,1) on pi -> implied logit(pi)` = qlogis(runif(1e5)),
       `N(0, 100^2) on logit(pi) -> implied pi` = plogis(rnorm(1e5, 0, 100)),
       `N(0, 1.5^2) on logit(pi) -> implied pi` = plogis(rnorm(1e5, 0, 1.5))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything()) |>
  ggplot(aes(value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~name, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "count")

The lesson: think about priors on the scale of quantities you understand, which is almost always the scale of the data, not the scale of the parameter.

3.2.2 Prior predictive checks

The practical way to do this is to simulate data from the prior, before looking at the real data:

\[ \theta^{(s)}\sim p(\theta),\qquad \tilde{\mathbf y}^{(s)}\sim p(\mathbf y\mid\theta^{(s)}),\qquad s=1,\ldots,S. \]

The \(\tilde{\mathbf y}^{(s)}\) are draws from the prior predictive distribution \(p(\tilde{\mathbf y})=\int p(\tilde{\mathbf y}\mid\theta)p(\theta)d\theta\). If simulated datasets look absurd (children with 40 malaria episodes per season), the prior is too vague or wrong.

Code 
S <- 5000
prior_pred <- tibble(
  prior = rep(c("Gamma(5, 2)", "Gamma(0.01, 0.01)"), each = S),
  lambda = c(rgamma(S, 5, 2), rgamma(S, 0.01, 0.01))) |>
  mutate(y_tilde = rpois(n(), lambda))

prior_pred |>
  group_by(prior) |>
  summarise(`P(y > 15)` = mean(y_tilde > 15),
            `P(y = 0)`  = mean(y_tilde == 0),
            `99.9% quantile` = quantile(y_tilde, 0.999))
# A tibble: 2 × 4
  prior             `P(y > 15)` `P(y = 0)` `99.9% quantile`
  <chr>                   <dbl>      <dbl>            <dbl>
1 Gamma(0.01, 0.01)      0.0146      0.952             97.0
2 Gamma(5, 2)            0           0.129             11

The supposedly “vague” \(\text{Gamma}(0.01,0.01)\) prior (common in older BUGS examples) predicts that about 95% of children have zero episodes and that 1 child in 1000 has well over 100 episodes in one season; \(\text{Gamma}(5,2)\) generates plausible data.

3.2.3 Prior sensitivity analysis

When in doubt, fit the model under several reasonable priors and report whether conclusions change. For the prevalence example of Lecture 1:

Code 
priors <- tribble(
  ~prior,                          ~a,   ~b,
  "Uniform Beta(1,1)",              1,    1,
  "Jeffreys Beta(0.5,0.5)",       0.5,  0.5,
  "Weakly informative Beta(2,5)",   2,    5,
  "Strong, sceptical Beta(10,40)", 10,   40)

priors |>
  mutate(post_mean = (a + k) / (a + b + n),
         lower = qbeta(0.025, a + k, b + n - k),
         upper = qbeta(0.975, a + k, b + n - k),
         `P(pi > 0.2)` = 1 - pbeta(0.2, a + k, b + n - k)) |>
  kable(digits = 3)
prior a b post_mean lower upper P(pi > 0.2)
Uniform Beta(1,1) 1.0 1.0 0.312 0.167 0.480 0.925
Jeffreys Beta(0.5,0.5) 0.5 0.5 0.306 0.160 0.477 0.910
Weakly informative Beta(2,5) 2.0 5.0 0.297 0.163 0.452 0.911
Strong, sceptical Beta(10,40) 10.0 40.0 0.238 0.151 0.336 0.780

The first three priors give almost identical conclusions; the strong prior (worth 50 children, centred on 20%) pulls the estimate down noticeably. That is not wrong, but it must be reported and justified.

3.3 Summarising the posterior

The posterior is the answer. For communication we summarise it.

3.3.1 Point estimates

A point estimate can be justified as the value minimising the posterior expected loss \(\int L(\theta,\hat\theta)\,p(\theta\mid y)\,d\theta\) (details in Appendix C):

Loss \(L(\theta,\hat\theta)\) Optimal estimate
Squared error \((\theta-\hat\theta)^2\) Posterior mean
Absolute error \(\lvert\theta-\hat\theta\rvert\) Posterior median
0-1 loss, \(1\) if \(\lvert\theta-\hat\theta\rvert\geq\epsilon\) and 0 otherwise, \(\epsilon\to0\) Posterior mode (MAP)

For skewed posteriors (variances, rates, odds ratios) the median is usually the most sensible single number. The MAP depends on the parameterisation and is not recommended as a default.

3.3.2 Credible intervals

A \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) credible interval \([l,u]\) satisfies \(P(l\leq\theta\leq u\mid\mathbf y)=1-\alpha\). Two common choices:

  • Equal-tailed (quantile-based) interval: \(\alpha/2\) posterior probability in each tail. Invariant to monotone transformations (the interval for \(e^\theta\) is the exponential of the interval for \(\theta\)).
  • Highest posterior density (HPD) interval: the narrowest region with the required probability; every point inside has higher density than every point outside. May be a union of intervals for multimodal posteriors. Not transformation-invariant.
Code 
post_a <- 5 + sum(y); post_b <- 2 + length(y)   # Gamma(45, 20) posterior

rbind(equal_tailed = qgamma(c(0.025, 0.975), post_a, post_b),
      HPD          = hdi(qgamma, 0.95, shape = post_a, rate = post_b))
                lower    upper
equal_tailed 1.641165 2.953397
HPD          1.611342 2.917067

Interpretation: given the model, prior and data, there is a 95% probability that the mean number of episodes per child lies in this interval. This is the statement people often (wrongly) attach to a frequentist confidence interval. Under a vague prior, the two intervals are frequently numerically close; their interpretations are not the same.

3.3.3 Posterior probabilities of clinically relevant events

Often more useful than any interval: \(P(\lambda>3\mid\mathbf y)\), \(P(\text{OR}<1\mid\mathbf y)\), \(P(\text{risk difference}>5\%\mid\mathbf y)\). These answer the questions decision-makers actually ask.

Code 
c(`P(lambda > 3 | y)` = 1 - pgamma(3, post_a, post_b),
  `P(lambda < 2 | y)` = pgamma(2, post_a, post_b))
P(lambda > 3 | y) P(lambda < 2 | y) 
        0.0189731         0.2343151

3.3.4 Bayes factors

For two hypotheses or models \(H_1,H_2\):

\[ \underbrace{\frac{P(H_1\mid\mathbf y)}{P(H_2\mid\mathbf y)}}_{\text{posterior odds}} =\underbrace{\frac{p(\mathbf y\mid H_1)}{p(\mathbf y\mid H_2)}}_{\text{Bayes factor }BF_{12}}\times \underbrace{\frac{P(H_1)}{P(H_2)}}_{\text{prior odds}}. \]

The Bayes factor is a ratio of marginal likelihoods \(p(\mathbf y\mid H)=\int p(\mathbf y\mid\theta,H)p(\theta\mid H)d\theta\). For composite hypotheses it can be extremely sensitive to the prior (a vaguer prior under \(H_1\) always favours \(H_2\)), and it is hard to compute for realistic models. For model comparison we will prefer predictive criteria (LOO, WAIC; Lecture 5). For questions about parameters, report posterior probabilities directly.

3.4 Prediction

The posterior predictive distribution for a new observation \(\tilde y\) averages the sampling model over posterior uncertainty in \(\theta\):

\[ p(\tilde y\mid\mathbf y)=\int p(\tilde y\mid\theta)\,p(\theta\mid\mathbf y)\,d\theta. \]

It is wider than \(p(\tilde y\mid\hat\theta)\) because it accounts for both the randomness of new data and our uncertainty about \(\theta\). Plugging in a point estimate \(\hat\theta\) ignores the second source and gives over-confident predictions.

For the Gamma-Poisson model the integral can be done analytically: \(\tilde Y\mid\mathbf y\sim\text{NegBin}\left(a+\sum y_i,\;\frac{b+n}{b+n+1}\right)\) (Appendix B.2). But the integral has a much simpler simulation form, which works for every model:

\[ \theta^{(s)}\sim p(\theta\mid\mathbf y),\qquad\tilde y^{(s)}\sim p(\tilde y\mid\theta^{(s)}). \]

Code 
S <- 1e5
lambda_s <- rgamma(S, post_a, post_b)          # 1. draw parameters from the posterior
y_tilde  <- rpois(S, lambda_s)                 # 2. draw new data given each parameter

tibble(k = 0:10) |>
  mutate(`simulation` = map_dbl(k, ~ mean(y_tilde == .x)),
         `exact NegBin` = dnbinom(k, size = post_a, prob = post_b / (post_b + 1)),
         `plug-in Pois(posterior mean)` = dpois(k, post_a / post_b)) |>
  pivot_longer(-k) |>
  ggplot(aes(k, value, fill = name)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:10) +
  labs(x = "episodes for a new child", y = "probability", fill = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

Simulation and exact answer agree; the plug-in Poisson is slightly too narrow. Two lines of code replaced a page of algebra.

3.5 Where closed forms run out: the normal model with unknown mean and variance

For \(Y_i\sim\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) with both parameters unknown, a fully conjugate prior exists (the normal-inverse-gamma, Appendix B.4), but it forces the prior uncertainty about \(\mu\) to be proportional to \(\sigma^2\), which is often unnatural. The more natural choice is an independent (semi-conjugate) prior

\[ \mu\sim\mathcal N(\mu_0,\tau_0^2),\qquad 1/\sigma^2\sim\text{Gamma}\left(\tfrac{\nu_0}{2},\tfrac{\nu_0\sigma_0^2}{2}\right), \]

for which the joint posterior \(p(\mu,\sigma^2\mid\mathbf y)\) is not a standard distribution. However, each full conditional distribution is standard:

\[ \mu\mid\sigma^2,\mathbf y\sim\mathcal N(\mu_n,\tau_n^2),\qquad 1/\sigma^2\mid\mu,\mathbf y\sim\text{Gamma}\left(\frac{\nu_0+n}{2},\;\frac{\nu_0\sigma_0^2+\sum_i(y_i-\mu)^2}{2}\right), \]

with \(\mu_n,\tau_n^2\) as in the table above. This is exactly the situation the Gibbs sampler (Lecture 3) is designed for. Almost every realistic model (regression with non-normal outcomes, random effects, missing data) is in this situation or worse, which is why the rest of the course is about computation.

NotePractical 2

Using conjugate results for a two-group comparison (number of children per woman, GSS data); prior predictive checks; prior sensitivity analysis; point and interval summaries (equal-tailed and HPD); posterior predictive distributions by simulation, compared with the exact negative binomial.

4 Lecture 3: Monte Carlo and Markov chain Monte Carlo

4.1 Monte Carlo integration

Almost every posterior quantity we care about is an expectation:

\[ E[g(\theta)\mid\mathbf y]=\int g(\theta)\,p(\theta\mid\mathbf y)\,d\theta. \]

Mean (\(g(\theta)=\theta\)), variance, probabilities (\(g(\theta)=I(\theta\in A)\)), and predictive probabilities are all of this form. If we can draw \(\theta^{(1)},\ldots,\theta^{(S)}\sim_{\text{iid}}p(\theta\mid\mathbf y)\), then by the law of large numbers

\[ \bar g_S=\frac1S\sum_{s=1}^S g(\theta^{(s)})\;\longrightarrow\;E[g(\theta)\mid\mathbf y]\quad\text{as }S\to\infty, \]

and by the central limit theorem the error is approximately normal with

\[ \text{MCSE}(\bar g_S)=\frac{\text{sd}(g(\theta))}{\sqrt S}. \]

The Monte Carlo standard error (MCSE) tells us how many digits of a simulation result we can trust. It shrinks like \(1/\sqrt S\), independently of the dimension of \(\theta\): this is why simulation beats grids.

Important

Keep two kinds of uncertainty apart. The posterior SD describes uncertainty about \(\theta\) and does not shrink as we simulate more. The MCSE describes numerical error in our summary and goes to 0 as \(S\to\infty\). Report posterior summaries; make sure the MCSE is small enough not to matter.

4.1.1 Example: comparing two groups

In the General Social Survey (Practical 2), the numbers of children of 40-year-old women without / with a college degree gave posteriors \(\theta_1\mid\mathbf y\sim\text{Gamma}(219,112)\) and \(\theta_2\mid\mathbf y\sim\text{Gamma}(68,45)\). Questions about functions of several parameters, which would need double integrals, become one-liners:

Code 
S <- 1e5
theta1 <- rgamma(S, 219, 112)
theta2 <- rgamma(S, 68, 45)

prob  <- mean(theta1 > theta2)
ratio <- theta1 / theta2

c(`P(theta1 > theta2)` = prob,
  MCSE = sqrt(prob * (1 - prob) / S),
  `median rate ratio` = median(ratio),
  quantile(ratio, c(0.025, 0.975)))
P(theta1 > theta2)               MCSE  median rate ratio               2.5% 
       0.973740000        0.000505672        1.298359083        0.997045199 
             97.5% 
       1.714282977

Once we have draws, every function of the parameters has a posterior distribution for free: rate ratios, risk differences, numbers needed to treat, predicted probabilities, rankings. Just compute the function for each draw.

Code 
tibble(S = round(10^seq(1, 5, length = 60))) |>
  mutate(estimate = map_dbl(S, ~ mean(rgamma(.x, 219, 112) > rgamma(.x, 68, 45))),
         mcse = sqrt(estimate * (1 - estimate) / S)) |>
  ggplot(aes(S, estimate)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = estimate - 2 * mcse, ymax = estimate + 2 * mcse), fill = "grey85") +
  geom_line(colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = prob, linetype = 2) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "number of Monte Carlo draws S (log scale)", y = "estimate of P(theta1 > theta2)")

4.2 Why we need MCMC

Monte Carlo needs independent draws from the posterior. We can get them when the posterior is a standard distribution, but usually all we can do is evaluate the unnormalised posterior

\[ \tilde p(\theta\mid\mathbf y)=p(\mathbf y\mid\theta)\,p(\theta), \]

pointwise, because the normalising constant \(p(\mathbf y)\) is an intractable integral.

Markov chain Monte Carlo constructs a sequence \(\theta^{(1)},\theta^{(2)},\ldots\) in which each value depends only on the previous one (a Markov chain), designed so that its long-run distribution (its stationary distribution) is the posterior. The price: the draws are dependent and the chain needs time to reach the posterior from its starting point. The payoff: we only ever need \(\tilde p\), never \(p(\mathbf y)\), since the constant cancels in ratios.

4.2.1 A non-conjugate example

Return to the malaria-episodes data but now put the prior on the log rate, which is natural if we later want to add covariates (Poisson regression):

\[ Y_i\mid\lambda\sim_{\text{iid}}\text{Pois}(\lambda),\qquad \lambda=e^{\theta},\qquad \theta\sim\mathcal N(0,1.5^2). \]

This prior is not conjugate; the posterior of \(\theta\) has no standard form. But its log is trivial to evaluate:

Code 
log_post <- function(theta) {
  sum(dpois(y, lambda = exp(theta), log = TRUE)) + dnorm(theta, 0, 1.5, log = TRUE)
}

For reference (and only because this is one-dimensional) we can also compute a grid answer:

Code 
theta_grid <- seq(-1, 2, length = 2001)
lp <- sapply(theta_grid, log_post)
grid_post <- exp(lp - max(lp)); grid_post <- grid_post / sum(grid_post * diff(theta_grid)[1])

4.3 The Metropolis algorithm

Starting from some \(\theta^{(0)}\), repeat for \(s=1,2,\ldots,S\):

  1. Propose \(\theta^*\sim\mathcal N(\theta^{(s-1)},\delta^2)\) (a random-walk step of size \(\delta\)).
  2. Compute the acceptance ratio \(r=\dfrac{\tilde p(\theta^*\mid\mathbf y)}{\tilde p(\theta^{(s-1)}\mid\mathbf y)}\); the unknown \(p(\mathbf y)\) cancels.
  3. Draw \(u\sim\text{Unif}(0,1)\). If \(u<r\) accept, \(\theta^{(s)}=\theta^*\); otherwise reject, \(\theta^{(s)}=\theta^{(s-1)}\).

Moves uphill (towards higher posterior density) are always accepted; moves downhill are accepted with probability \(r\). The chain therefore spends time in each region in proportion to its posterior probability. On the log scale step 3 becomes: accept if \(\log u<\log\tilde p(\theta^*)-\log\tilde p(\theta^{(s-1)})\).

Code 
metropolis <- function(log_target, n_iter, init, step) {
  theta <- numeric(n_iter)
  theta[1] <- init
  lp_current <- log_target(init)
  n_accept <- 0
  for (s in 2:n_iter) {
    proposal <- rnorm(1, mean = theta[s - 1], sd = step)
    lp_proposal <- log_target(proposal)
    if (log(runif(1)) < lp_proposal - lp_current) {
      theta[s] <- proposal; lp_current <- lp_proposal; n_accept <- n_accept + 1
    } else {
      theta[s] <- theta[s - 1]
    }
  }
  list(theta = theta, acceptance_rate = n_accept / (n_iter - 1))
}

set.seed(1)
run <- metropolis(log_post, n_iter = 20000, init = -1, step = 0.3)
run$acceptance_rate
[1] 0.5134257

That is the whole algorithm: sixteen lines of R. Does it work?

Code 
keep <- run$theta[-(1:1000)]      # discard the first 1000 iterations (burn-in)

ggplot() +
  geom_histogram(aes(x = keep, y = after_stat(density)), bins = 60,
                 fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  geom_line(aes(theta_grid, grid_post), colour = "salmon", linewidth = 1) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1.3)) +
  labs(x = expression(theta == log(lambda)), y = "density",
       subtitle = "histogram: Metropolis draws; line: grid approximation")
Code 
c(post_mean_lambda = mean(exp(keep)), quantile(exp(keep), c(0.025, 0.975)))
post_mean_lambda             2.5%            97.5% 
        2.204286         1.576547         2.911583

4.3.1 Tuning the step size

The algorithm is correct for any step size \(\delta>0\), but its efficiency depends strongly on \(\delta\):

Code 
set.seed(2)
runs <- map_dfr(c(0.02, 0.3, 5), function(d) {
  r <- metropolis(log_post, n_iter = 2000, init = -1, step = d)
  tibble(step = paste0("step = ", d, " (acceptance ", round(100 * r$acceptance_rate), "%)"),
         iteration = seq_along(r$theta), theta = r$theta)
})

ggplot(runs, aes(iteration, theta)) +
  geom_line(colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~step, ncol = 1) +
  labs(y = expression(theta))
  • Too small: nearly every proposal is accepted but the chain crawls; it takes hundreds of iterations to leave the (bad) starting value and successive draws are almost identical.
  • Too large: most proposals land in the tails and are rejected; the chain sticks for long stretches.
  • About right: the trace looks like a “hairy caterpillar”. For random-walk Metropolis, acceptance rates of roughly 20-50% are a good target (about 44% in one dimension, decreasing towards 23% in many dimensions).

Software such as NIMBLE tunes \(\delta\) automatically during an adaptation phase.

4.3.2 Metropolis-Hastings

If the proposal distribution \(q(\theta^*\mid\theta)\) is not symmetric (for example, proposals on the log scale for a positive parameter), the ratio needs a correction:

\[ r=\frac{\tilde p(\theta^*\mid\mathbf y)\,q(\theta^{(s-1)}\mid\theta^*)}{\tilde p(\theta^{(s-1)}\mid\mathbf y)\,q(\theta^*\mid\theta^{(s-1)})}. \]

This is the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm. For a symmetric proposal the \(q\) terms cancel and we recover Metropolis. The correction ensures detailed balance, \(p(\theta)T(\theta\to\theta^*)=p(\theta^*)T(\theta^*\to\theta)\), which guarantees that the posterior is the stationary distribution of the chain.

4.4 The Gibbs sampler

When the parameter is a vector \(\boldsymbol\phi=(\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_p)\) and every full conditional \(p(\phi_j\mid\text{all other parameters},\mathbf y)\) is a distribution we can sample from, update one component at a time, always conditioning on the most recent values:

\[ \begin{aligned} \phi_1^{(s)}&\sim p\left(\phi_1\mid\phi_2^{(s-1)},\phi_3^{(s-1)},\ldots,\phi_p^{(s-1)},\mathbf y\right)\\ \phi_2^{(s)}&\sim p\left(\phi_2\mid\phi_1^{(s)},\phi_3^{(s-1)},\ldots,\phi_p^{(s-1)},\mathbf y\right)\\ &\;\;\vdots\\ \phi_p^{(s)}&\sim p\left(\phi_p\mid\phi_1^{(s)},\phi_2^{(s)},\ldots,\phi_{p-1}^{(s)},\mathbf y\right) \end{aligned} \]

Gibbs sampling is a special case of Metropolis-Hastings in which the proposal is the full conditional itself, and every proposal is accepted (\(r=1\)).

4.4.1 Example: haemoglobin with unknown mean and variance

Haemoglobin (g/dL) measured in 20 pregnant women at an antenatal clinic (simulated data):

Code 
set.seed(42)
hb <- round(rnorm(20, mean = 10.8, sd = 1.4), 1)
n_hb <- length(hb); ybar <- mean(hb)
c(n = n_hb, mean = ybar, sd = sd(hb))
        n      mean        sd 
20.000000 11.070000  1.824425

Semi-conjugate priors from Lecture 2: \(\mu\sim\mathcal N(12,2^2)\) and \(1/\sigma^2\sim\text{Gamma}(\nu_0/2,\nu_0\sigma_0^2/2)\) with \(\nu_0=1\), \(\sigma_0=1.5\). The Gibbs sampler alternates between the two full conditionals:

Code 
gibbs_normal <- function(y, S, mu_init, sigma2_init,
                         mu0 = 12, tau0_2 = 4, nu0 = 1, sigma0_2 = 1.5^2) {
  n <- length(y); ybar <- mean(y)
  mu <- sigma2 <- numeric(S)
  mu[1] <- mu_init; sigma2[1] <- sigma2_init
  for (s in 2:S) {
    # 1. mu | sigma2, y  ~ Normal
    tau_n2 <- 1 / (1 / tau0_2 + n / sigma2[s - 1])
    mu_n   <- tau_n2 * (mu0 / tau0_2 + n * ybar / sigma2[s - 1])
    mu[s]  <- rnorm(1, mu_n, sqrt(tau_n2))
    # 2. 1/sigma2 | mu, y ~ Gamma   (uses the NEW value mu[s])
    shape <- (nu0 + n) / 2
    rate  <- (nu0 * sigma0_2 + sum((y - mu[s])^2)) / 2
    sigma2[s] <- 1 / rgamma(1, shape = shape, rate = rate)
  }
  tibble(iteration = 1:S, mu = mu, sigma = sqrt(sigma2))
}

set.seed(3)
gs <- gibbs_normal(hb, S = 5000, mu_init = 6, sigma2_init = 20)   # deliberately poor start
Code 
p1 <- ggplot(gs[1:30, ], aes(mu, sigma)) +
  geom_path(colour = "grey50") + geom_point(colour = "salmon") +
  geom_density_2d(data = gs[-(1:500), ], colour = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "first 30 Gibbs steps", x = expression(mu), y = expression(sigma))
p2 <- gs |> pivot_longer(c(mu, sigma)) |>
  ggplot(aes(iteration, value)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.2, colour = "steelblue") +
  facet_wrap(~name, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") + labs(title = "trace plots", y = NULL)
gridExtra::grid.arrange(p1, p2, ncol = 2)
Code 
gs[-(1:500), ] |>
  summarise(across(c(mu, sigma), list(mean = mean, lo = ~quantile(.x, 0.025), hi = ~quantile(.x, 0.975))))
# A tibble: 1 × 6
  mu_mean mu_lo mu_hi sigma_mean sigma_lo sigma_hi
    <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>      <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>
1    11.1  10.3  11.9       1.88     1.37     2.64

The path moves in axis-parallel steps (one parameter at a time), quickly leaves the poor starting point, and then wanders around the posterior. Note how the first few iterations are clearly not representative of the posterior: they should be discarded as burn-in (also called warm-up).

4.5 Beyond Metropolis and Gibbs

Real software combines and extends these building blocks:

  • Metropolis-within-Gibbs: update each parameter (or block of parameters) in turn, by a Gibbs step if its full conditional is standard, by a Metropolis step otherwise. This is essentially what NIMBLE and JAGS do by default.
  • Block updating: update strongly correlated parameters jointly (e.g. all regression coefficients), with a multivariate random-walk or slice sampler. One-at-a-time updates move very slowly along narrow diagonal ridges.
  • Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) and its adaptive version NUTS use the gradient of \(\log\tilde p\) to propose distant moves that are still likely to be accepted. They scale much better to high dimensions and correlated posteriors. HMC/NUTS is the engine of Stan (and brms), and is available in NIMBLE through the nimbleHMC package.
  • Approximate methods that avoid sampling altogether (integrated nested Laplace approximation, INLA; variational inference) are fast for particular model classes, at the cost of being approximations.

4.6 When MCMC struggles

Things to watch for (they motivate the diagnostics of Lecture 4):

  • Starting values far from the posterior: need a longer burn-in; use several chains from dispersed starting values.
  • Strong posterior correlation between parameters, e.g. intercept and slope when a covariate is not centred: one-at-a-time samplers mix slowly.
  • Multimodality: a chain can get stuck in one mode; different chains may find different modes.
  • Weakly identified parameters (vague priors + little data): the chain drifts over huge ranges.
  • “Funnels” in hierarchical models (Lecture 5): the scale of some parameters depends strongly on another parameter.
NotePractical 3

Monte Carlo estimation and MCSE; posterior predictive probabilities by simulation (GSS data); writing your own Metropolis sampler for a Poisson model with a normal prior on the log rate, tuning the step size; extending it to two parameters (Poisson regression with one covariate); writing a Gibbs sampler for the normal model.

# Helper: convert a coda mcmc.list into a long data frame (for ggplot trace plots)
mcmc_to_long <- function(samples) {
  purrr::imap_dfr(samples, function(ch, i) {
    as_tibble(as.matrix(ch)) |>
      mutate(chain = factor(i), iteration = row_number())
  }) |>
    pivot_longer(-c(chain, iteration), names_to = "parameter")
}

trace_plot <- function(samples, pars = NULL) {
  d <- mcmc_to_long(samples)
  if (!is.null(pars)) d <- filter(d, parameter %in% pars)
  ggplot(d, aes(iteration, value, colour = chain)) +
    geom_line(alpha = 0.6, linewidth = 0.3) +
    facet_wrap(~parameter, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) +
    labs(x = "iteration (after burn-in)", y = NULL)
}

# Preliminaries

## How this course is organised

The course is built around one idea: **a Bayesian analysis is a posterior distribution, and in practice we obtain posterior distributions by computing, not by integrating by hand.** Mathematics is kept to what you need to understand *what* the computer is doing and *why* it can go wrong.

| Lecture | Topic | Main computational tool | Practical |
|:-:|:--|:--|:--|
| 1 | Bayesian reasoning: prior, likelihood, posterior | Grid approximation | 1 |
| 2 | Priors, conjugate models, posterior summaries & prediction | Exact formulae + simulation | 2 |
| 3 | Monte Carlo and Markov chain Monte Carlo | Hand-written Metropolis & Gibbs samplers in `R` | 3 |
| 4 | MCMC in practice: `NIMBLE` and convergence diagnostics | `NIMBLE`, `posterior` | 4 |
| 5 | Bayesian regression, model checking, comparison, hierarchical models | `NIMBLE`, `loo` | 5 |

Longer derivations (conjugate posteriors, Jeffreys priors, the full normal model, loss functions) are in the **appendices**. You might be asked to derive a sonjugate prior in the exam, but for the other derivations, while they are useful for understanding and for self-study, you are not expected to be able to reproduce them in the exam.

## Code notes

* These notes have been prepared using `quarto` - qmd shared on GitHub.

* All code is `R`; Bayesian models are specified in `NIMBLE` (a dialect of `BUGS`).

* `R` packages used: `tidyverse`, `gridExtra`, `HDInterval`, `nimble`, `coda`, `posterior`, `loo` (plus `MCMCvis` optionally). Install them all before the first practical: `NIMBLE` needs a working C++ compiler (Rtools on Windows, Xcode command line tools on macOS).

* Course materials: <https://github.com/gitMarcH/UNIMA_STA623_2026>
